entities.summary:
Damjing, or Donchó, was a Korean Buddhist priest who was sent to ancient Japan from Goguryeo around 610. He was tasked with establishing Buddhism in Japan and played a crucial role in the country's early Christianization. Damjing's mission was part of a larger exchange of ideas and cultures between Goguryeo and Japan, which was facilitated by the Silk Road and the maritime trade routes of the time.


Damjing's significance lies in his ability to bridge the cultural and religious divide between Korea and Japan, and to introduce Buddhism to a new and receptive audience. His legacy can be seen in the many Buddhist temples and artifacts that dot the Japanese landscape, and in the enduring influence of Buddhism on Japanese art, literature, and philosophy.


Despite the passage of centuries, Damjing's story remains a fascinating and little-known chapter in the history of East Asian Christianity. His bravery and determination in the face of cultural and religious hostility serve as a powerful reminder of the enduring power of faith and conviction.


The discovery of Damjing's tomb in 2012 provided a unique window into the life and times of this enigmatic figure. The tomb's contents, including a beautifully crafted bronze coffin and a number of Buddhist artifacts, offer a poignant glimpse into the spiritual practices and cultural traditions of ancient Japan.
